TRUE/FALSE?). > **Structure** = the container holding many values (vector? data frame? list?). Everything today hangs off that sentence. You already know how to insert a chunk (**Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + I**, from last week). Whenever you see **"➕ insert a chunk"**, make one — every YT today depends on it. {{< vspace 1.5rem >}} # 1 · Data types (30 min) ## 1.1 · The types, defined first (before any code) (5 min) Every single value in R has a **type**. Here are the ones you'll live with, each with a Cal Poly example: | Type | What it is | Example value | |---|---|---| | **numeric** (double) | a number that can have decimals | `4.75` — a latte at Julian's | | **integer** | a whole number (written with an `L`) | `38L` — people in the Rec Center at 7 am | | **character** | text, in quotes | `"Scout Coffee"` | | **logical** | `TRUE` or `FALSE` | `TRUE` — the drink is iced | | **factor** | text from a *fixed menu* of allowed values | `"morning"` from {morning, afternoon, evening} | | **Date** / **date-time** | a calendar date; a date *and* clock time | `2026-09-22` / `2026-09-22 07:00:00` | | **NA** | a missing value — a hole, not a type of its own | the headcount nobody recorded | ## 1.2 · Finding the type with `class()` (7 min) **LM1 — `class()` tells you the type (4 min).** Predict each `class()` from the table above, *then* run: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM1: predict from the table, then run class(4.75) # Julian's latte ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(38L) # people in the Rec Center at 7 am ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "integer" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class("Scout Coffee") # where the latte came from ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(TRUE) # iced? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "logical" ``` ::: ::: > *Q1. Predictions: ____ · ____ · ____ · ____* **LM2 — doubles vs integers (1 min).** Both are numeric; `typeof()` tells them apart. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM2 typeof(4.75) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "double" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} typeof(38L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "integer" ``` ::: ::: **LM3 — dates and date-times (2 min).** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM3 today <- Sys.Date() class(today) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Date" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} right_now <- Sys.time() class(right_now) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt" ``` ::: ::: ## 1.3 · Three families: quantitative, categorical, other (6 min) R's types sort into three families you'll use to pick plots and summaries all term: | Family | Question it answers | R types | Cal Poly examples | |---|---|---|---| | **Quantitative** | *how much? how many?* — you can average it | numeric, integer | latte price (`4.75`), Rec Center headcount (`38`), miles from campus (`2.3`) | | **Categorical** | *which kind? which group?* — you count it | character, factor, logical | coffee shop (`"Julian's"`, `"Starbucks"`, `"Scout"`), time slot (`"morning"`), iced (`TRUE`) | | **Other** (time/date) | *when?* — ordered, but not a plain number | Date, date-time | the day you bought the latte, the clock time you swiped into the Rec | > *Q2. Which family: (a) the number of people in the Rec Center at 5 pm · > (b) the shop that made your latte · (c) the date of the game vs. UCSB · > (d) whether you bought a latte today (yes/no)?* > > *Your answer:* (a) ____ · (b) ____ · (c) ____ · (d) ____ **A small distinction — "string" vs "character".** Other languages call text a *string*. R calls the *type* **character**, and one piece of text (`"Scout Coffee"`) is a **string** — a character value of length one. So `"latte"` is a string, its class is character, and `c("latte", "mocha")` is a character *vector* of two strings. You'll hear both words; they are not in conflict. ## 1.4 · Factors vs characters — why it matters (6 min) **LM4 — the same text, two types (4 min).** Rec Center headcounts come with a time slot. As character, the slots are just words; as a **factor**, they come with a fixed menu of allowed values (**levels**) *in an order you choose*: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM4: character vs factor slot_chr <- c("evening", "morning", "afternoon", "morning", "evening", "evening") slot_fct <- factor(slot_chr, levels = c("morning", "afternoon", "evening")) class(slot_chr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(slot_fct) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "factor" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} levels(slot_fct) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "morning" "afternoon" "evening" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} table(slot_chr) # alphabetical — afternoon first ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` slot_chr afternoon evening morning 1 3 2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} table(slot_fct) # the order YOU chose — morning first ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` slot_fct morning afternoon evening 2 1 3 ``` ::: ::: > *Q3. How many levels does `slot_fct` have, and what order did we give > them? Why would that order matter on a bar chart?* > > *Your answer:* **LM5 — NA, the missing value (2 min).** `airquality` (built in) has real missing ozone readings; `is.na()` finds them and `sum()` counts them: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM5: count the missing values in Ozone sum(is.na(airquality$Ozone)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 37 ``` ::: ::: > *Q4.
